text: Knowing when an LLM is wrong: an introduction to LM-Polygraph, and what uncertainty estimators cost
Ahmad Bin Qasim
Problem: Confidently wrong
Confidently wrong
A wrong answer arrives with the same certainty as a right one.
Four of the 7B model's BioASQ answers. Each is wrong against the reference, and each got a probability above 0.98 from the model itself. Nothing in the text of an answer says which ones to check.
What an uncertainty score is for
Rank the answers, flag the least certain, and what is kept gets better.

Accuracy of the answers kept as the most uncertain are flagged for review, ranked by mean token entropy. Flagging half of them lifts the kept accuracy from 45% to 67%. A useless score stays on the flat line; a perfect one follows the upper dashed line. AUROC, used in the results, measures how well the ranking separates right from wrong.
Background: Where the uncertainty is
Five places to look for doubt
Every estimator reads one of five signals, and each needs different access to the model.

White-box needs the model's probabilities or internals; black-box needs only its text. Families and method names follow Vazhentsev et al. (arXiv:2605.14570); self-report is added here because p(True) is in the run. T1–T4 are this talk's cost tiers.
Reading the probabilities
One forward pass, and the model has already said how sure it was.
All three come out of the pass that produced the answer, so they cost nothing beyond generation. They need the token probabilities, which many hosted APIs do not return.
Asking the model
A second prompt asks the model to judge its own answer.
p(True) reads the probability the model puts on “True”; the empirical variant samples the verdict ten times and counts. Both cost one more prompt per answer, which is tier 2.
Asking again
If repeated samples disagree, the first answer was a guess.

Sample several answers to the same question and measure how far they agree: by shared words, or by meaning, with an NLI model testing whether two answers entail each other. Sampling is tier 3; the NLI model on top is tier 4. White-box variants also weight each sample by its probability.
Training a detector
A classifier on the model's hidden states can learn what a wrong answer looks like — given labels.
Probes need graded answers from the task they will be used on, and a new set for every new task or model. They are named here for completeness and were not run.
Tooling: LM-Polygraph
LM-Polygraph
One library runs every one of these estimators behind one interface.
Open source, pip-installable. An estimator returns one uncertainty score per answer, higher meaning less sure; grading the answers and scoring the estimators against them is a separate step.
Methods: The four cost tiers
The same methods, priced
The tiers sort these methods by what they cost, not by what they read.

Every estimator in the results, placed by signal type and cost tier. Tiers are cumulative: a tier-4 run also pays for tiers 1–3. Sampling methods split across tiers 3 and 4 by whether they also need the NLI model.
Methods: BioASQ, and grading it
Results: What works, and what it costs
Every estimator, ranked
The cheapest tier holds both the winner and the traps.

AUROC for separating wrong answers from right ones, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Blue is tier 1 — one forward pass, no sampling and no second model. Hollow markers are sign-inverted: they return a confidence rather than an uncertainty, and read as 1−AUROC.
What each cost tier buys
Paying more buys consistency, not a higher ceiling.

Each dot is one estimator, placed in its cost tier; the bar is the tier median. Tiers are cumulative, so the step from one column to the next is the marginal cost of that tier — a second forward pass, then sampling, then a DeBERTa NLI model over the sample set.
The scores behind the AUROC
Cheapest against dearest — the overlap looks much the same.

Raw uncertainty scores for every question, split by whether the answer was graded correct. An AUROC in the high 0.7s still means two heavily overlapping distributions: this is a triage signal, not a verdict.
The same methods on a bigger model
The ranking survives scale; the task gets harder.

Every method's AUROC on the smaller model against the larger one. Points cluster along the diagonal — the ranking transfers — but most sit below it, so the stronger model's residual errors are harder to catch even though it is right more often.
